newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Congress power struggle to slow Brazil re-election.
newsitem.headline: Congress power struggle to slow Brazil re-election.

text.p: A special committee in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies was due to begin debating this week a proposed constitutional amendment that would give President Fernando Henrique Cardoso the chance of a second term.

But progress on re-election may be hesitant as several other issues distracted lawmakers, principally an unusually bitter struggle among government allies to preside over the two houses of Congress, observers said.
"As usual, it's the allies and not the opposition that are going to make life hard for the government," said a congressional official who asked not to be named.

The lower house committee has 40 sessions -- each one equivalent to a working day -- to debate and vote on a proposal that Brazilian presidents, state governors and mayors be allowed to stand for a second consecutive term.
Newspapers said the committee would hold its first meeting October 29, but real progress was only expected after the November 15 second round of voting in municipal elections.

The re-election issue might also be complicated by resentment among congressmen over plans to include them in a 10,800 real pay ceiling for public sector workers included in the government's civil service reform.

The government hopes that by calling an extraordinary session of Congress to run through the December 15-February 15 recess the re-election bill might clear the committee and reach the floor of the chamber by January.
The government wants re-election through the volatile lower house before its pro-reform president Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes is replaced on February 1 by an as yet unknown successor.
But the struggle to replace Magalhaes and Jose Sarney, his counterpart in the Senate, is already causing friction within the government's fragile alliance.
Normally, the two biggest parties in Congress -- the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and the Liberal Front Party (PFL) -- take turns running each house.
But both contests look set to go to a vote this year after the PMDB announced it would not give up the Senate and allow powerful PFL boss Antonio Carlos Magalhaes to take over.
"If the PMDB doesn't get its way, it could torpedo Fernando Henrique's re-election dream," said a PMDB aide.

In the lower house race, the PMDB is split between two would-be candidates, pro-reform Michel Temer and anti-Cardoso Antonio Paes de Andrade, while the PFL leader in the chamber, Inocencio Oliveira, is considered to have an outside chance.
"I expect there may be some agreement by January, which is when the re-election debate will start heating up," said Carlos Lopes of consultants Santafe Ideias.
Cardoso would be best advised to avoid any involvement in the congressional elections that might turn one of the two powerful parties against his re-election plans, Lopes said.
"There's a chance things could explode, but in Congress everything can be negotiated," he said.
